identity.title: Observations of highly inclined disks with ALMA: Results from <SUP>12</SUP>CO gas and continuum observations

paper_type_evidence.quote: We present ALMA high angular resolution band 7 (0.9 mm) continuum images and [12] CO (3-2) gas moment maps as well as HST and VLT/SPHERE scattered light images.

In this paper, we focus on 5 new highly inclined disks in Ophiuchus, Upper Scorpius and Lupus, in both millimeter continuuum and [12] CO gas (Project 2022.1.00742.S, PI: F. Ménard). CO data for 9 disks from the previous survey are also included.

question.value: Study the radial and vertical extents of 12CO gas, millimeter dust continuum, and optical/NIR scattered light in 14 highly inclined protoplanetary disks to constrain radial drift and vertical settling, and estimate dynamical stellar masses.

evidence.quote: We aim to study the radial and vertical extents of [12] CO gas, millimeter dust thermal emission and optical/near infrared scattered light by dust in highly inclined protoplanetary disks.
Additionally, we aim to provide estimates of the dynamical stellar masses including those for which no prior measurements exist.

This study is a follow up of the survey presented in Villenave et al. (2020) which combined several observing programs in Taurus, Ophiuchus and Chamaeleon (Projects 2013.1.01175.S, 2016.1.01505.S, 2016.1.00771.S, 2016.1.00460.S, PIs: C. Dougados, F. Louvet, G. Duchêne and F. Ménard).

We also include Band 6 12 CO (2-1) observations of Oph 163131 from projects 2016.1.00771.S (PI: G. Duchêne) and 2018.1.00958.S (PI: M. Villenave).
The second part of this survey is based on ALMA observations from project 2016.1.00460.S (PI: F. Ménard), for which the continuum images have previously been published in Villenave et al. (2020).

We also include Band 6 12 CO (2-1) observations of Oph 163131 from projects 2016.1.00771.S (PI: G. Duchêne) and 2018.1.00958.S (PI: M. Villenave).

In this context, the ongoing DiskStrat ALMA Large Program (Project 2024.1.01212.L, PI: R. Le Gal) will provide critical observations to improve our characterization and understanding of highly inclined disks.

analysis_steps.goal: Measure ALMA continuum and 12CO radial extents

method.value: Extract surface brightness profiles along the major axis integrated over the vertical extent and normalized by peak intensity. For 12CO, visually select the channel with maximum radial extent on blue and red sides in the image cube. Measure diameter at 3-sigma above background noise.

evidence.quote: To measure the radial extent of the disks from their continuum emission we extracted surface brightness profiles along the major axis of each disk. We integrated over the full vertical extent
The major axis size was determined at a level of 3σ above the background.
Instead of processing all the channels for which the [12] CO emission is detected, we visually selected the channel for which the radial extent is maximum, for the blue and red side to maximize SNR.

evidence.quote: The major axis size was determined at a level of 3σ above the background.

validation.value: Uncertainty estimated by varying the integration window size and quadratically adding 1/10 of the beam size along the major axis; compared cube cuts against Moment 0 maps.

evidence.quote: Therefore, we estimated the associated uncertainty by varying the window over which the profile is estimated and quadratically added a tenth of the beam size along the major axis direction.
We note that a few of these values are larger by up to 40% (in the most pathological case) than those estimated from the moment 0 maps due to differences in noise statistics and cloud contamination

analysis_steps.goal: Measure ALMA continuum and 12CO vertical extents and disk inclinations

method.value: Extract minor-axis brightness profiles. For continuum, fit a Gaussian to obtain FWHM and quadratically subtract beam FWHM. Estimate inclination from axis ratio using major axis size at 50% peak flux (or ellipse fit to ring for Lup 160708). For 12CO, collapse all channels with detected emission and measure minor-axis extent at 3-sigma without Gaussian fitting.

evidence.quote: The profiles being single peaked because the continuum vertical extent is not well resolved, we estimated the FWHM by fitting Gaussians to the disk profiles except for Lup 160708 where the ring geometry prevents a measurement of the intrinsic vertical extent.
We also quadratically subtract the FWHM of the beam from the measured FWHM to obtain the intrinsic FWHM and propagated the errors.

We have chosen to collapse all channels for which the gas emission was detected to gain SNR. To estimate the gas vertical extent, we followed the same method as for the radial extent of the gas without fitting Gaussians to the disk profiles

analysis_steps.goal: Estimate dynamical stellar masses and systemic velocities from PV diagrams

method.value: Construct position-velocity (PV) diagrams and superimpose 3 Keplerian velocity curves (fitting outermost maximum intensity for lower limit, signal-to-noise transition for preferred mass, and off-signal for upper limit) while visually aligning systemic velocity symmetrically.

evidence.quote: With a coarse exploration, we thus choose to add 3 Keplerian velocity curves: a first one which fits the outermost maximum intensity of the PV diagram, a second one which follows the transition between the signal and the noise and a last one clearly off the signal.

claims.hypothesis: Radial drift and optical depth effects cause protoplanetary disks to be radially larger in gas than in micron-sized dust, and larger in micron-sized dust than in millimeter-sized dust (R_gas > R_dust,um > R_dust,mm).
claims.experiment: Measured and compared 3-sigma major-axis diameters of 14 highly inclined disks in ALMA 12CO, HST/VLT optical/NIR scattered light, and ALMA millimeter continuum.
claims.result: 11 of 14 disks follow R_gas > R_dust,um > R_dust,mm (the other 3 have R_dust,mm > R_dust,um); R_gas / R_dust,mm is ~1.5-2 for highly inclined disks compared to 2-3 for less inclined disks (90% Mann-Whitney U and 93% KS confidence).
claims.finding: Most disks follow R_gas > R_dust,um > R_dust,mm, and highly inclined disks show smaller gas-to-mm-dust radius ratios than less inclined disks due to line-of-sight integration enhancing outer mm continuum detection, consistent with optical depth effects and/or radial drift.

evidence.quote: The majority of disks in our sample (11 out of 14) follow R gas - R dust, µm - R dust, mm . The other 3 disks, including 2 in multiple systems, appear more extended in millimeter continuum than in scattered light.

claims.hypothesis: Millimeter-sized dust grains settle vertically toward the disk midplane while micron-sized dust remains coupled to the gas.
claims.experiment: Measured minor-axis vertical extents of 12CO gas (at 3-sigma), optical/NIR scattered light (spine separation), and millimeter continuum (deconvolved Gaussian FWHM) across the sample.
claims.result: All disks follow H_gas >> H_dust,mm (with H_gas ~ 3-6 H_dust,mm for most disks), while most disks have H_gas ~ 2-3 H_dust,um and a few have H_gas ~ H_dust,um.
claims.finding: Millimeter dust is strongly settled in the midplane and decoupled from the gas, while micron-sized dust is not fully coupled to the gas in most disks.

evidence.quote: Regarding the vertical extent defined as the apparent emitting height, most disks in our sample follow H gas - H dust, mm . This strengthens our previous findings that the millimeter dust is highly decoupled from the gas and forms a layer in the disk midplane due to vertical settling.
Most disks appear more vertically extended in gas than in scattered light, suggesting that the µm-sized dust is not fully coupled to the gas.
The majority of the disks follow H gas ≈ 3–6 H dust,mm, indicator of strong dust settling.

claims.hypothesis: The correlation between disk radius and millimeter continuum or 12CO line flux is a geometrical effect arising because disks are optically thick.
claims.experiment: Compared disk radii against scaled submillimeter continuum and 12CO (3-2) line fluxes before and after dividing fluxes by cos(i) to correct for projection effects.
claims.result: Highly inclined disks are fainter than lower-inclination disks at a given radius; applying the 1/cos(i) correction aligns highly inclined disks with low-inclination disks and increases the Pearson correlation from r = 0.47 (91%) to r = 0.66 (99.1%) for continuum and from r = 0.67 (99.2%) to r = 0.71 (99.5%) for 12CO.
claims.finding: The tightened correlation after inclination correction confirms that both millimeter continuum and 12CO line emission are optically thick in most disks.

evidence.quote: This is also observed in our sample of highly inclined disks, where the two quantities are significantly correlated ( r = 0.47 and r = 0.67) with confidence levels of 91% and 99.2% based on Pearson tests for the continuum and line emission, respectively.

For highly-inclined disks, the confidence level in the correlation between millimeter flux and disks increases to 99.1% and 99.5% ( r = 0.66 and r = 0.71 from Pearson tests) for the continuum and line emission, respectively.
Overall, these results provide strong support for the optical depth interpretation of the radius-flux correlation for both continuum and line emission.

claims.hypothesis: Stellar gravity dominates the vertical extent of the gas disk and stellar mass correlates with disk radius.
claims.experiment: Estimated dynamical stellar masses from 12CO position-velocity diagrams and performed Pearson correlation tests with gas aspect ratio (h/r) and disk radius.
claims.result: Dynamical mass is anti-correlated with gas aspect ratio h/r (r = -0.49, ~91% confidence level), whereas no significant correlation is found between dynamical mass and millimeter dust disk radius (~62% confidence level) or gas radius.
claims.finding: Higher-mass stars host thinner gas disks due to stronger gravitational pull, while disk radius does not correlate with dynamical stellar mass in this sample.

evidence.quote: We found an anti-correlation between the dynamical mass and the aspect ratio, emphasizing the dominant role of gravity in setting the disk vertical extent, but no correlation with the disk radius.

why_this_data.value: Highly inclined disks allow direct measurement of vertical extents with minimal de-projection, and line-of-sight integration compensates for low optical depth in faint outer regions; 3 disks from Villenave et al. (2020) were excluded due to an envelope, CO outflow, or circumbinary nature.

evidence.quote: Highly inclined disks are the best objects for this study because their vertical extent is more directly accessible, with minimal de-projection required.
Moreover, highly inclined disks can provide better constraints on the disk outer radii because of the line-of-sight integration which compensates the low optical depth in the fainter outer regions.

We choose to not include 3 disks from the previous survey either because of the presence of an envelope, a CO outflow, or because of the circumbinary nature of the source (IRAS 04302, HH 30, and IRAS 04158 respectively).

why_this_method.value: Dynamical masses from PV diagrams are independent of stellar models and viewing geometry (where edge-on disks block photospheric light); 12CO radial extents were measured on visually selected peak-extent channels in cubes rather than Moment 0 maps because Moment 0 maps suffer from noise statistics and cloud contamination; visual Keplerian curves were used on PV diagrams because modest SNR, cloud contamination, and substructures preclude a robust statistical approach.

evidence.quote: If possible, estimating the dynamical mass thanks to the interaction between the host star and the gas of the disk in rotation is the most reliable method to determine this parameter independently of stellar models or viewing geometry

We note that a few of these values are larger by up to 40% (in the most pathological case) than those estimated from the moment 0 maps due to differences in noise statistics and cloud contamination, confirming the inadequacy of moment maps to estimate the full radial extent of disks.

limitations_admitted.value: Dedicated radiative transfer models for highly inclined disks are lacking to disentangle radial drift from optical depth effects and to reconstruct vertical temperature profiles.

evidence.quote: Models of radial drift with radiative transfer dedicated to highly inclined disks are required to disentangle between radial drift and opacity effects based on the R gas / R dust, mm ratio.

A thorough interpretation of this anti-correlation will require full radiative transfer models tailored to each system, as well as tomographic reconstruction of their vertical temperature profile (e.g., Dutrey et al. 2017; Flores et al. 2021), which is beyond the scope of this study.

referee_caveats_inferred: Dynamical masses are estimated visually by overplotting 3 Keplerian curves on PV diagrams rather than forward-modeling 3D radiative transfer and kinematics in the visibility or image cube domain; the derived masses are systematically 30-50% higher than literature values.

3-sigma isophotal sizes (and visual selection of peak-extent channels for 12CO) depend on sensitivity and SNR rather than a flux-fraction metric (e.g., R_68 or R_90) commonly used in the low-inclination literature comparison samples.
Applying a 1/cos(i) geometric correction to edge-on disks (i > 80-88 deg) diverges as i approaches 90 deg and neglects emission from the optically thick vertical outer wall/flared surface.
